vignette: Malik was twenty-four when the convoy breached the dry brushlands of eastern Syria, a civilian corridor that erupted in coordinated mortar fire. He remembered the dry grass igniting into a rolling wall of flames that cut off their escape, and the desperate, shouted corrections from his fixer who pushed him toward cover seconds before a rocket impacted nearby. Malik believed the command structure had abandoned them, echoing the sharp criticisms of supervisors back home who had questioned his judgment before the mission even began. He walked out through the charred landscape, the scent of smoke clinging to his jacket long after evacuation. The specific geometry of the ambush-the way the flames herded them and the fixer's frantic corrections mirrored the tactical debriefs-made every subsequent exposure to smoke and natural terrain instantly potent. Returning to Ohio, he took a park ranger posting near the Appalachian foothills, where the natural world quickly became a minefield. Walking through dense pine groves or watching a campfire flicker at the edge of his vision spiked his pulse, leaving him unable to relax even when he knew he was miles from danger. That physiological alarm kept him awake, trouble falling or staying asleep becoming routine, while any delayed shift change made him certain disaster was already underway. Because these environmental cues reliably triggered such raw alarm, he began cutting off all contact with friends and family. He started drinking heavily after every patrol to dull the edges, avoided every uniform and weapon he could find, and kept his cabin locked against the past. The constant dread fed a survival guilt that he had only lived through luck, a creeping sense that he was isolated and set apart, and a conviction that he had acted in ways that violated his own deepest values. The cycle soon tightened across his daily routine. His sleep problems and inability to relax left him with no mental buffer, so he retreated further into isolation, leaned on his bottles, and avoided every uniform and weapon. That spike of threat amplified his guilt over those perceived moral compromises, deepening his sense of isolation and values violation. The conviction that he had violated his own values made him interpret a hiker's casual feedback as a devastating critique, instantly pulling the fire and terrain triggers into sharp focus. That threat made the sight of fire and open brush feel suffocating, while the unrelenting alarm kept him hyper-vigilant to any correction. Yet the longer he stayed away from his brother's calls, the more certain he became that he was fundamentally broken and had compromised his moral code. Avoiding structure left him adrift, making him hyper-aware of any criticism, which instantly reignited the fire and terrain alarms. He drank to quiet the paranoia, but the alcohol left him exhausted, which meant he slept even worse, which made his physiological alarm constant. Now at forty-seven, the cabin's isolation has become his cage. He finally scheduled an intake after a minor brush fire sparked by a camper's spark sent him fleeing to his truck, sitting there shaking while his phone buzzed with unanswered calls from his brother. He came to the clinic hoping to break the paralysis, terrified he might never walk a forest without dread, but desperate to prove he hadn't lost the man he was before the desert burned.
